column11: notes

column2: 80 vacant positions eliminated and filled faculty and staff cuts announced — FY2027 raises suspended
column11: 80 vacant positions eliminated (35 open faculty + 45 open staff) plus unspecified cuts to filled faculty and staff positions. FY2027 merit salary increases suspended entirely. President Edward Feser announced July 1. Enrollment fell more than 2,000 students (15%) YoY — 13,307 undergraduate/post-baccalaureate students for year ending May 2026. S&P Global revised bond outlook to "negative" June 23 citing inability to maintain enrollment and revenue. Third consecutive round of SLU cuts: Round 1 (October 2024) — 23 layoffs + 130 vacancies frozen under Pestello; Round 2 — balanced budget FY2025 (no major new layoffs); Round 3 (this action). Feser: "Revenue realities mean the university will need to operate with fewer people and resources." Strategic plan draft forthcoming. Filled position cuts not quantified publicly — total impact higher than 80. Separate from April 2026 tennis program cuts also in database.

column2: 43 academic majors and minors eliminated — replaced by dozens of workforce-focused certificates
column11: 43 academic majors and minors eliminated as part of academic redesign at Pennsylvania Western University (formed from merger of Edinboro, California, and Clarion universities of Pennsylvania in 2022). Simultaneously adding dozens of new workforce-focused certificates. PennWest California campus arts programs specifically named in article headline. Part of broader restructuring of the system created by the 2022 merger of three PASSHE universities. Specific program names not available from metadata alone — article paywalled. PASSHE system facing enrollment and funding pressures across all campuses.

column2: 9 degree programs discontinued unanimously including Gender Studies, Urban Planning and Applied Math
column11: Board of Trustees voted unanimously June 25 (two separate motions) to discontinue all 9 programs identified by Provost Lorenzo Smith. Programs discontinued: BA Gender, Women's and Sexuality Studies (CIP 05.0207); BA Urban and Regional Planning (CIP 4.0201); BA International Affairs (CIP 45.0901); BA Applied Technology; BA Data Science (CIP 11.0401); BA English as a Second Language (CIP 13.1401); BA Early Childhood and Special Education (CIP 13.1001); MA Interdisciplinary Studies; MS Applied Mathematics (CIP 27.0301). Faculty Senate recommended saving GWSS, Urban Planning, International Affairs, and Applied Technology — overruled by provost and president. Provost Smith recommended all 9 discontinued June 18; President McMahan passed to board same day. Programs averaged under 10 graduates/year over past 5 years. Mathematics and Anthropology removed from original 11-program list early due to enrollment projections. Urban Planning had highest declared incoming freshmen: 2. Many courses will continue as minors. Current declared majors may complete degrees. Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown appeared in February in support of GWSS program — overruled. Part of second major round of EWU cuts; prior round took place 2024-25 school year. Fall 2025 enrollment: just under 10,000 students. EWU is only Spokane County-headquartered public university.

column2: 110 administrative staff laid off as federal research portfolio continues to shrink
column11: 110 employees primarily in administrative functions laid off across Bloomberg School of Public Health, Carey Business School, and central administration. "As our federal research portfolio shrinks the infrastructure around it must change in parallel" — spokesperson Doug Donovan. Prior cost-management: hiring freeze, pausing raises for employees earning $80K+, reducing discretionary spending, eliminating vacant positions, 20% reduction in 5-year capital project spending — all proved insufficient. JHU simultaneously increasing in-house research awards by $50M and nearly doubled lobbying spending since 2024. Hiring freeze continues. Second distinct layoff round — separate from March 2025 USAID-driven 2,200 cuts also in database. Trump administration terminated $6.9B-$8.2B in university grants nationally per Center for American Progress.

column2: Downtown Library, LibTech lending desk and Curriculum Materials Center closed with no notice
column11: Three library units closed simultaneously June 25 with zero advance notice: Addition Financial Downtown Campus Library (served 20+ downtown-exclusive majors including Legal Studies and Health Informatics); LibTech desk at John C. Hitt Library (laptops, DSLR cameras, tablets, microphones, lighting kits, calculators — free equipment loans for students); Curriculum Materials Center on main campus (PreK-12 materials for education majors and local teachers). Staff informed by HR in person or by phone day-of — some mid-shift; told not to return. UCF HR explicitly planned to give no advance warning to "limit the upset." UCF cited "comprehensive review of library usage, academic priorities, and available resources." Actual reason per Florida Rep. Anna Eskamani: UCF did not receive expected preeminence status funding from Tallahassee ($10M+ annually for faculty raises and services). Prior closure: Universal Orlando Foundation Library at Rosen College of Hospitality Management permanently closed April 25, 2025. Student workers also terminated without notice. Main campus John C. Hitt Library and downtown tech lending desk remain open. Students directed to UCF Libraries feedback form and Board of Trustees meetings. 73,000+ student enrollment — one of the largest universities in the US.

column2: 20 positions eliminated to close $6.5M FY2027 budget deficit
column11: Board approved FY2027 budget June 23 eliminating 20 currently occupied positions out of ~900 full-time employees (~2.2% of workforce). Budget gap: $4M projected revenue increase vs $10.5M expense increase = $6.5M deficit. Working group of faculty, staff and administrators found $12.9M in total cuts (exceeding deficit). Missouri facing $1.5-2B state general revenue shortfall; higher ed leadership advised to prepare for at least 10% state appropriations cut for FY2028 — equal to ~$5M for SEMO. President Hodson contract extended through June 30, 2030. Board also approved stadium Phase II design contract with OSPORTS (designs due December 2026). No academic programs eliminated in this round.

column2: Health Sciences Division dissolved — 28 positions eliminated in final integration phase
column11: Health Sciences Division administrative structure permanently dissolved effective August 7, 2026 — final phase of year-long realignment. ~28 positions eliminated. All programs folded directly into existing university units: Interprofessional Clinical and Professional Skills Center + Center for Transformative Interprofessional Healthcare + Arizona Area Health Education Centers + Indigenous health programs → under new provost-selected supervisors. Clinical and Translational Science Institute + Arizona Center for Accelerated Biomedical Innovation → Office of Research and Partnerships. Clinical Placements and Partnerships → Mel and Enid Zuckerman College of Public Health. Interprofessional K-12 Initiatives + All of Us Research Program → College of Medicine Tucson. Room scheduling → Office of the Registrar. Interim VP Jennifer Barton returning to research (cancer imaging tools). Health Sciences budget $48.6M following 18% cut last year — unclear how funds will be allocated post-restructuring. Provost Prelock: "reduce administrative redundancy and build a leaner structure." HR offering affected employees assistance finding other UA positions. No academic programs eliminated — all health sciences programs continue under new administrative homes.

column2: 30+ positions eliminated including 14 faculty — 401(k) matching discontinued to save $4.4M
column11: 30+ total employees severed including 14 of ~200 faculty members. 401(k) matching program also discontinued. Saves $4.4M against $5M projected budget shortfall. President Brian McAulay announced June 16 via email calling decisions "difficult but necessary." Root cause: chiropractic flagship program placed on CCE probation in 2024 for 77% licensing exam pass rate (below 80% threshold) — probation lifted January 2026 after 100% winter pass rate. But enrollment disruption persists: 2,289 students fall 2025 (lowest in 10+ years), down 11% YoY; chiropractic college enrollment down 16%. 90%+ of revenue comes from tuition; chiropractic program provides 75% of operating revenue — making university extremely sensitive to enrollment shifts. Doctor of Chiropractic costs ~$200K; undergraduate ~$55K. Moody's downgraded bond rating March 2026 with "negative" outlook. 439 full-time employees fall 2024 (federal data). One of the largest chiropractic programs nationally. Marietta GA; private non-profit. Prior actions: Rosen College library at UCF closed same week in similar dynamic of post-preeminence budget pressure.

column2: 31 positions eliminated across multiple units as part of budget reductions
column11: Internal emails obtained by Cap Times confirm 31 positions being eliminated across multiple UW-Madison units. Cuts include: Division of Information Technology (DoIT) — layoffs and position eliminations; University Communications — staff reductions; Office of Sustainability — significant cuts; Wisconsin Public Media (WPM) — positions eliminated including programming staff. Additional measures: travel restrictions, hiring freezes, reduced discretionary spending. Driven by flat state funding, federal research grant reductions, and rising operational costs. Separate from the 100-160 potential Extension layoffs (WARN Act court filing, April 2026) which remain contingent on court ruling over USDA funding freeze — those are captured in a separate database entry. Chancellor Jennifer Mnookin has not yet made a formal campus-wide announcement about the full scope of cuts.

column2: 7 degree and certificate programs discontinued as part of regular program review
column11: Board of Governors approved discontinuation of 7 programs June 10: BS Computer and Information Security, MS Cyber Forensics and Security, MA Journalism, Graduate Certificates in Digital Communications, Digital Forensics, Integrated Strategic Communications, and Media Management. 4 of the 7 (Journalism MA, Digital Communications, Media Management, Integrated Strategic Communications certificates) had enrollment suspended since 2022 and were already in teach-out. Part of routine program review process. Budget deficit reduced from $28M to $10M; projected to fall below $3M over next year with help of Huron consulting firm assessing organizational alignment, revenue opportunities, and inefficiencies. Metro Tuition rate expanded to all border states by 2028 to attract out-of-state students. President Smith cited "three Ds" — demographic cliff, digital disruption, and doubt about higher ed value — as challenges Marshall is navigating.

column2: Baking & Pastry Arts, Culinary Arts and Paralegal programs eliminated — 4 faculty affected
column11: Board voted unanimously June 9 to eliminate 3 programs: Baking and Pastry Arts, Culinary Arts, and Paralegal. 3 faculty in food programs laid off via reduction-in-force vote (Culinary Arts Professor Emily Wallace, Baking and Pastry Arts Professor Melanie Shelton, Culinary Arts Professor J.P. Downey-McCarthy); Paralegal faculty member retired (4 total). Food programs cost college $618K/year combined; cited low enrollment and low earning potential for graduates — no formal education required for entry-level positions. Affected students may complete programs via teach-out. Nearly 20 students and community members spoke in favor of food programs at board meeting. Professors argued for restructuring not elimination — proposed changes would save $250K/year and create self-sustaining budget; board did not adopt. Programs described as serving marginalized communities including students of color, queer and trans students, neurodivergent students. Professor Wallace has already found new job at Bremerton School District launching culinary program for high school students. $3.4M-$4M budget shortfall driven by tuition not keeping pace with salary/benefits growth — personnel costs now 83% of budget. President Timothy Stokes called decisions "incredibly difficult."

column2: 5 majors and 4 minors sunsetted plus 15 voluntary separations under Doane Forward plan
column11: Majors sunsetted fall 2027: New Media, Strategic Communication, Policy and Values, Ethics and Interfaith Studies, Human Relations. Minors sunsetted: Film, Journalism, Communicating Quantitative Information, Communication/Environmental Communication. ~80 students affected on Crete campus and online — all may finish current pathways. 15 faculty/staff took voluntary separation packages; teaching faculty retained through 2026-27 to complete teach-out. Savings amount not disclosed; departments asked to prepare 13-20% budget reduction drafts (April 2026). Part of "Doane Forward" 6-month strategic plan developed with stakeholder input. Simultaneously building new innovation center covering engineering, business, AI, computer science, data analytics and mathematics — developed with input from CEOs. New 4-year engineering + 1-year MBA pathway in development. President Hughes cited national trend: "every month, a school like Doane will close." Private liberal arts institution in Crete NE. Also: Nebraska Wesleyan University (not in database) eliminated 14 staff and reduced 3 positions to part-time in October 2025.

column2: 40 positions eliminated and athletic scholarships reduced to cut $10M in spending
column11: 40 total positions eliminated as part of $10M spending reduction target. No major academic programs eliminated; biblical languages major discontinued; College of Online Learning restructured to integrate with main degree programs (May 2026). Athletic scholarships reduced — average scholarships for student athletes to near $16K starting 2026-27. University remains on federal watch list for shaky financial stability. Assemblies of God-affiliated institution; ~2,000 students; Springfield MO. Prior rounds: 2023 saw 44 employees affected (32 retirement buyouts + 12 layoffs); 2014 saw 25 positions cut in post-consolidation restructuring with Assemblies of God Theological Seminary and Central Bible College. Raised $117M+ in "Here Now" fundraising campaign over 4 years; invested in AGFinancial Arena and Walther Hall renovation. Discontinued employee tuition discount for dependents in 2025-26. Restructuring part of broader effort to grow enrollment using freed-up funds.

column2: Political Science, Childhood Development and Music programs eliminated under SB 185 financial exigency law
column11: Board of Regents approved elimination of 3 programs June 8: Political Science, Childhood Development, and several Music areas. Affected students offered teach-out plans. CPE Academic and Strategic Initiatives Committee approved full recovery plan June 9. Undergraduate enrollment projected to drop 9% fall 2026 and 20% by spring 2027. Under Kentucky Senate Bill 185 (passed spring 2026 declaring KSU in "financial exigency"): university transitioning to polytechnic institution focused on STEM and healthcare; limited to 10 academic areas of study (applied sciences, health sciences, natural sciences, humanities, engineering and technology). Many liberal arts programs shifting online and taught entirely by adjunct faculty. New admission requirements: minimum 2.5 GPA + 18 ACT composite score. Stricter tuition enforcement: students with $1,000+ outstanding balance for 30+ days barred from enrolling; debts referred to KY Dept of Revenue; federal/state tax refunds intercepted for debts over $1,000 past 60 days. President granted authority to terminate any employee including tenured faculty with 30 days notice. Two active lawsuits seeking to block SB 185; judge allowed academic changes to continue pending final ruling. Kentucky's only public HBCU; founded 1886; land grant institution. Polytechnic restructuring does not change HBCU status. CPE President Thompson: "We are not just killing programs — we are reengineering liberal arts to work with our polytechnic focus."

column2: Westminster Conservatory band and orchestral instrument departments discontinued after 56 years
column11: Westminster Conservatory of Music (Princeton) band and orchestral instrument departments discontinued — all instructors effectively let go including 29-year clarinet/saxophone faculty Ken Ellison, 48-year flute faculty Amy Wolfe, 20-year piano/assistant director Marianne Lauffer, and others. Piano, voice, recorder, honors music, Opera Outings, and Westminster Community Orchestra programs relocated to Rider's Lawrence Township campus (not discontinued). Band and orchestral instrument instruction (strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion) eliminated entirely — no space at Lawrence Township campus. Conservatory founded 1970 on former Westminster Choir College campus; part of Rider since 1992. Municipality of Princeton acquired the 22-acre campus April 2025; stated it was not consulted and learned of decision simultaneously with general public June 8. Decision described as "purely operational" by Rider Senior Associate Dean Vodlicka — spending significantly more than revenue on the Princeton-based programs. Part of $21.8M deficit Rider has faced in recent years. Faculty given opportunity to meet with administration June 9; Rider exploring partnerships with other area organizations to continue private lessons.

MA in Literature (CIP 23.0101) eliminated — only 8 students enrolled at time of closure, down from 16 in 2018. Final cohort completing degrees; no new admissions. MA in Economics (CIP 45.0601) also eliminated. Moratorium on minors in Chinese Studies (~10 students) and Irish Studies (~7 students). Students in eliminated programs describe feeling abandoned mid-degree with limited job market options for humanities graduates. One student said she feels her degree is now "worthless on paper." Faculty acknowledged the difficult position students are in but noted financial pressures left no alternative. Originally proposed January 28, 2026 pending Faculty Senate and Commissioner of Higher Education approval — both approvals now confirmed. Part of broader UM response to $18M FY27 budget shortfall; university also cut fewer than 10 staff via layoffs. UM MFA in Creative Writing continues unaffected. UMaine System approved 10 other program suspensions/eliminations this fiscal year across other campuses.

column2: 11 positions eliminated campuswide amid enrollment and cost pressures
column11: 11 employees laid off across several departments and programs campuswide. University cited "operational and financial pressures" including enrollment realities and rising costs. Affected employees informed directly and privately. Simultaneous dining services transition to Sodexo Campus partnership (effective June 1) impacted 45 workers — ~90% hired by Sodexo. These are separate from the 11 direct layoffs. Private university founded 1836; ~1,843 students; $203M endowment. President Mark Zupan. Part of broader NY private institution financial pressures.

column2: 16 positions eliminated — roughly 1% of workforce — as part of strategic restructuring
column11: ~16 employees laid off week of June 2 — roughly 1% of ~1,600-person total workforce. University may also eliminate additional vacant positions as restructuring continues. Part of broader reallocation toward functions aligned with long-term strategy. Provost announced required 15% budget cut for Academic Affairs by end of FY2028 (November 2025). Library collections budget decreasing from $2.6M to lower level as part of same cuts. Driven by federal and state funding cuts, enrollment shifts, and industry demand changes. Specialist STEM institution in Golden CO; known for engineering, applied sciences, and energy research. Separate from CSU Fort Collins ($35.8M cuts) and CSU Pueblo (9 positions) also in database — all part of Colorado higher ed funding squeeze.

15% of full-time workforce laid off — 400-460 total positions eliminated through layoffs and vacant position cuts. Layoff notices handed out June 2, 2026. Four colleges consolidated into two: Eugene Lang + New School for Social Research merged into one unit; Parsons + College of Performing Arts + Schools of Media merged into second unit. PhD admissions paused across nearly all doctoral programs for 2026-27 including sociology, philosophy, economics, politics. Student medical services gutted. Prior actions: 7% reduction via voluntary buyouts (Dec 2025); 40% of full-time faculty received voluntary separation/early retirement offers (169 academics — AAUP called it largest attempted faculty firing in the nation); S&P downgraded bond rating February 2026 citing deep deficits. Deficit variously reported as $48M structural deficit / $60M operating deficit. Mandate from board: balanced budget by FY2028. 20% enrollment decline since 2021. Parsons + College of Performing Arts alumni rallied repeatedly throughout year. Full-time faculty facing 15% reduction. President Joel Towers; Provost Richard Kessler. Originally in database from March 2026 Hyperallergic article when status was rumor.

column2: Center for a Regenerative Future closed after 3 years of budget-driven decline
column11: Center for a Regenerative Future (CRF, formerly Center for Sustainability) closing June 30 after 3 years of budget-driven decline. Formerly housed thrift store, bike shop, gear garage, food pantry, climate cafes, community dinners, graduate gown recycling, and 40-student paid internship program (now reduced to 2 interns). Undergraduate program director position cut spring 2024 triggering collapse of thrift store. Bike shop and gear garage absorbed by Basecamp. Food pantry restructured under Student Affairs and Inclusive Excellence. Part of DU administration effort to reduce $10M from non-academic units amid $20-30M budget deficit. Faculty senate passed no-confidence vote in Chancellor Haefner (May 2026). Remaining staff hosting "Living Funeral" June 5 to redistribute materials to campus organizations.

column2: 36 nonfaculty staff eliminated — 15% of nonfaculty workforce in second round of cuts
column11: 26 full-time + 10 part-time nonfaculty staff eliminated June 1 — 15% of nonfaculty workforce. Saves ~$3.5M. Combined with faculty cuts ($3M) and contract/other savings ($1M+) = ~$7.5M of $10M goal reached. Additional savings: Berman Museum annual funding cut from $600K to $300K; advertising and cleaning contracts changed; software changes; consultants eliminated; annual alumni awards ceremony ended; family and homecoming weekends combined; staff credit card purchasing tightened. President Graml: "We have to be leaner in order to really focus on the student mission." Running total of Ursinus cuts in 2025-26: 29 faculty + 36 staff = 65 total positions eliminated.

column2: 32 academic advising positions eliminated as part of advising system redesign
column11: 32 academic advising positions eliminated as part of university advising system redesign. Notably some employees were previously laid off, then rehired, and are now losing their jobs again in this second round. University stated "any reductions in force are difficult." Cuts are administrative staff positions — advisers who support student academic planning and degree completion. No academic programs eliminated.

column2: 66 positions eliminated including 29 layoffs to address $20M structural deficit
column11: 29 employees laid off + 37 vacant positions eliminated (66 total). Reorganization follows 2-year Huron Consulting Group assessment and Operation Excellence Initiative. Work groups identified $18M in savings across academic programs, compensation/benefits, technology and endowment. Prior signals: hiring freeze Dec 2025-May 2026 for vacant positions; 2025 benefit cuts; graduate revenue below projections; insurance and utility costs rose sharply. Second-largest private university in Maryland (~4,000 undergrad, 1,900 grad). Jesuit institution. President Sawyer said Loyola is "well-positioned for the future." Part of Maryland higher ed wave: UMD College Park (150 jobs), Bowie State ($18M deficit), UMB (60 positions), Morgan State all cutting simultaneously due to $111M state funding reduction.

column2: 6 tenured faculty laid off — fourth round of cuts since January 2025
column11: Wednesday May 27 layoffs fell on 6 tenured faculty in School of Communication and Culture and School of Design. Fourth round of faculty layoffs since January 2025 — prior rounds: 48 full-time faculty total (32 tenured) since Jan 2025, plus 70 staff in 2024. Part of ongoing effort to close $40M+ deficit amid declining enrollment. Layoff notices described as coming without prior warning to affected faculty. Running total since 2024: 70 staff + 54 faculty laid off. President Bolton simultaneously hiring new senior leadership (5 new VP-level hires in spring 2026) — Chronicle noted tension between cuts and new hires. Admin restructured May 2 into 5-dean oversight model. No further rounds ruled out.

column2: Men's and women's tennis programs discontinued following coach departure
column11: Men's tennis ended immediately; women's tennis continues through 2026-27 then discontinued. Longtime head coach Bert Poole departing for another coaching opportunity — his exit triggered the decision to end both programs. Division III institution; member of ODAC (Old Dominion Athletic Conference). Women's tennis recently fell 4-0 to No. 13 Washington and Lee in ODAC championship.

column2: BA in Religious Studies eliminated; multiple zero-enrollment minors and certificates closed
column11: UH System Board of Regents approved closure of BA in Religious Studies at May 22 quarterly meeting. 15 students enrolled; 5 not actively pursuing degree. Failed to meet Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board threshold of 25 graduates over 5 years. Religious studies minor remains; religion courses continue in core curriculum and as electives. No faculty layoffs — professors retained. Part of Texas SB 37 compliance review: additional closure of multiple minors and certificates across UH System (UH, UH-Clear Lake) with zero enrollments for past 5 years. Simultaneously approved new BA in Philosophy, Politics and Economics and new BS in Biological Sciences. Provost Chase cited statewide and national trend of declining religion/biblical studies enrollment. Prior language program cuts at UH: German, Italian, French (over past 10 years). Board also delegated expanded contracting authority to Chancellor Khator.

column2: 11 core faculty and ~40 instructor positions eliminated to address structural deficit
column11: President Paul Burkhardt sent letter to staff and faculty announcing elimination of 11 core faculty positions and ~40 instructor jobs to correct long-term structural operating deficit. Burkhardt acknowledged "these sorts of reductions are very difficult, and they cause suffering." Separate April 17, 2026 announcement introduced tuition reset for fall 2026 (lower per-credit rate for new students, flat for current) and new Ponderosa Plan strategic framework for long-term sustainability. New online and low-residency programs added simultaneously. Buddhist-inspired nonsectarian liberal arts institution founded 1974; ~1,100 students. Known as birthplace of modern mindfulness movement.

column2: 21 programs and minors eliminated — second round of cuts in 3 years to close $8.1M deficit
column11: 10 undergraduate programs, 4 graduate programs, and 7 minors discontinued. Named programs: Mathematics (BA/BS), Physics (BA/BS), Economics (BA/BS), and others. 171 total students affected (111 majors + 60 minor students) — less than 5% of total enrollment; only 25 are incoming fall 2026 students. All current and incoming accepted students can complete degrees via teach-out. Second major round of cuts: prior 2024 round eliminated 12 programs including French, Spanish, Philosophy, and Early Childhood Education. $8.1M structural deficit being addressed through program cuts and enrollment growth strategy. Deficit reduced by nearly half since 2023. Graduate enrollment up ~50% over 3 years driven by new programs (Clinical Mental Health Counseling: 65 students). Courses required for other majors will continue to be offered. President Stephen H. Kolison Jr. cited need to focus resources on high-demand growing programs.

WARN Act notice filed April 1 for 167 employees (110 full-time, 57 adjunct/part-time) effective June 1 — ~34% of workforce. Board of Trustees voted May 15 to suspend all residential undergraduate in-person classes while continuing online programs. Students given 48 hours notice to vacate campus housing. ~350 traditional undergrad students told to find alternative arrangements. Graduate and online programs continue. University simultaneously exploring sale of carbon capture patent and seeking investor group to acquire institution. President Dempsey said board hopes to reopen traditional programs fall 2026 but could not guarantee it. Indiana Commission for Higher Education notified; transfer pathways being developed. Private General Baptist institution founded 1885. Financial collapse attributed to years of enrollment decline, deferred maintenance, and failed fundraising campaigns.

column2: 3 programs discontinued and 2 paused amid 7% budget reduction and Washington funding crisis
column11: Programs discontinued: Administrative Office Systems, Paralegal, Multimedia. Programs paused fall 2026 pending enrollment strategy review: Automotive Service Technician, Family Life Education. Construction Trades program (previously under review) retained with updated curriculum, expanded lab, new equipment, and community donations. Furloughs planned July 2026 for exempt and classified employees earning $90K+/year as one-year stabilization measure. College already reduced overall budget ~7% over past year including closure of Fort Worden campus. New programs proceeding despite cuts: Dental Hygiene, K-8 Teacher Education, and mobile workforce training — all supported by external grants, partnerships, and philanthropy. Driven by rising operating costs and Washington state community college funding challenges. President Suzy Ames said review involved Board of Trustees, President's Cabinet, faculty leadership, and employees. Serves Clallam and Jefferson counties.

column2: 35 programs eliminated and 10 faculty laid off to address $20M deficit
column11: 35 total programs eliminated: 28 undergraduate majors and minors + 7 graduate programs. Named majors cut: Health Education, Economics, Human Resources, International Business, Mild/Moderate Educational Needs, Music Theory, Physics, Sociology, Sustainability. 10 faculty laid off as a result. Deficit grew from initial $3M estimate to $20M. Second major round: prior cuts in late 2024 saw 35 faculty/staff laid off or offered buyouts (~7% of teaching base). Former faculty cited toxic work environment, HR complaints not followed up, secretive reasoning for cuts. President Lee Fisher announced via May 9 email to faculty/staff following May 8 board meeting. Private liberal arts and conservatory institution in Berea, OH.

column2: 3 majors eliminated and 66 positions cut to close $5M deficit after Deloitte review
column11: Board voted May 9 to approve restructuring plan. 3 academic programs permanently eliminated: Music, International Studies, and Gender/Sexuality/Women's Studies (125 combined student majors). Creative Writing merged into English department. 9 other academic units consolidated. ~66 total positions eliminated: faculty in eliminated/consolidated programs + administrative restructuring. Saves $5M annually — satisfying Oregon HECC requirement for balanced long-term plan tied to $15M emergency state funding (approved February 2026). Deloitte analysis found top 3 units (business, education, psychology) represent 45% of headcount; top 10 programs = 78% of enrollment; 10 units operated at a loss. Outsourcing of administrative functions to Oregon flagship universities or third-party providers also approved. Average course enrollment minimum raised from 16 to 22 students. 56 faculty had signed letter disputing Deloitte data quality prior to vote. Board chair thanked community for input during "difficult but necessary" process. Part of Oregon higher ed funding crisis — state ranks 14th from bottom in per-FTE spending. Prior year: SOU cut 23 programs and laid off 18 employees.

column2: Energy and Environmental Research Center cuts 27 positions, furloughs 13 amid federal funding delays
column11: EERC (Energy and Environmental Research Center) at UND cut 27 positions and furloughed 13 (full or temporary basis) from ~210-person workforce. Furloughed employees may be reinstated based on operational needs and funding. Cuts driven by multi-year delays in federal funding — primarily from U.S. Dept of Energy — compounded by Trump administration spending curbs. FY2025 budget ~$85M: $40M competitive federal grants, $30M private sector, remainder state sources. COO Tom Erickson told legislators in January: "We are waiting for the funds that were promised to us over a year ago." EERC designated North Dakota's State Energy Research Center; research spans coal, oil, natural gas, biomass, carbon capture, geothermal, nuclear, and EVs. Hosted Energy Secretary Chris Wright in 2025. UND and NDSU representatives previously told legislators Trump-era spending cuts already cost ND millions in research funding.

UTA confirmed via email to faculty/staff and statement to WFAA that it will suspend new admissions into some programs and consolidate overlapping degree pathways in others. Changes affect fewer than 200 of 42,700+ enrolled students. All currently enrolled/admitted students can complete degrees without disruption; individualized advising and transition options will be provided. Suspending new admissions: BA in Art History, MS in Sustainable Building Technology, MS in Taxation (certificates, elective courses, and minors in these programs remain available). Consolidations/mergers: BA Chemistry → BS Chemistry, BA Geology → BS Geology, BA Mathematics → BS Mathematics, BA Theatre Arts → BFA Theatre Arts, MA Mathematics → MS Mathematics. Admissions suspended pending interdisciplinary curriculum revision: BA Anthropology, Master of Engineering, MS in Materials Science and Engineering. UTA cited faculty engagement and data-driven analysis. Review conducted by a representative faculty group. UT System Board of Regents policy "Abandonment of Academic Positions or Programs" permits the university president to eliminate programs absent financial exigency, citing low enrollment, redundancy, program quality, and student outcomes. Academic program review initiated in 2025 to align offerings with student demand, workforce needs, and long-term institutional sustainability.
column24: The University of Texas at Arlington

column2: 79 positions eliminated amid second consecutive multimillion-dollar deficit
column11: President Aminta Breaux announced elimination of 79 total positions through reorganization, vacancy cuts, and direct layoffs — ~6% of 1,175-person workforce. Second consecutive deficit: $13.6M shortfall in prior year (resolved via hiring delays and vacant position cuts); now facing $18M deficit for 2026-27. Maryland's oldest HBCU, founded 1865. Prior year deficit addressed without layoffs; this round requires direct workforce reduction. Breaux stated decisions made "with care, thoughtfulness and deep respect for faculty, staff and students." Specific breakdown of faculty vs staff positions not disclosed in available reporting.

column2: $35.8M in strategic cuts including staff layoffs and 0.5% workforce reduction
column11: CSU System board approved FY2027 budget May 7-8 with $35.8M in strategic cuts at Fort Collins campus: staff layoffs (0.5% of workforce) + $3M from eliminating vacant positions. Financial aid tied to tuition costs preserved; 3% merit raise pool maintained for faculty/staff. Driven by Colorado state budget flat-funding higher ed to close $1.5B state deficit (constitutional balanced budget requirement). Tuition for in-state students capped at 3.5% increase by state. President Parsons called flat funding "a real reduction in resources" due to cost increases. Fall headcount rose 2% to 34,096 students between 2019-2024 — one of the healthier enrollment pictures in Colorado.

column2: 96 UK employees laid off due to federal grant terminations in medicine and HIV programs
column11: 96 employees in UK College of Medicine Department of Behavioral Science and UK Healthcare HIV Program Operations laid off effective June 30 due to discontinuation of federal grant funding. UK will try to help affected employees find other positions at the university; all employees receive 60 days notice and pay per WARN Act. Separate from 926 Aramark Campus LLC dining/concessions contractor layoffs (also effective June 30) — those are third-party contractor employees, not UK staff, and Aramark/UK expect most to transition to new provider. UK ending 12-year Aramark partnership and exploring new enterprise services provider for dining and concessions.

column2: INSPIRE first-year student success program shut down due to lack of funding
column11: INSPIRE (Incoming Student Program for Inclusion, Retention, and Excellence) shutting down after spring 2026 semester. Established 2022; served first-year students with small cohorts, GE course support, financial planning, schedule planning, and faculty/peer connections. Particularly impactful for first-generation college students. Shut down due to lack of funding amid CSU system-wide budget crisis ($1B+ projected CSU deficit for 2026-27). CSUEB enrollment down ~26% since 2016. Mock funeral protest held by students and staff on campus. Separate ongoing cuts include Theater and Dance department merger/closure threat (1,400+ signature petition), Art program course cuts, and ART 242 elimination affecting graduating students.

column2: Permanent institution closure after 43 years due to enrollment challenges
column11: Physical campus at 1725 E. David Road closed May 4, 2026; instruction ends June 2; permanent closure June 23, 2026. Founded 1983 by Tim Potter as School of Advertising Art; rebranded to Modern College of Design in 2017-18 following $6M expansion adding 23,000 sq ft. President Jessica Barry (since 2007, purchased college 2013) cited inability to support operations due to enrollment challenges despite efforts to evolve. ~211 students enrolled (federal data); 92% acceptance rate; 59% graduation rate. Offered bachelor's and associate degrees in graphic design. Record enrollment of 214 in 2024-25 school year — closure came despite recent enrollment growth. No summer semester; summer tuition/fees to be refunded. Transfer agreements with local/online design programs being developed. Virtual commencement June 7; diplomas mailed after. Students unable to complete may apply for Closed School Discharge (federal student loan forgiveness). Career services available through June 23. Building valued at ~$3.8M per county records.

column2: 4 programs eliminated under Ohio SB1 mandate, 19 total cut since 2024
column11: Most recent round eliminated 4 programs: BA Public Health (merged into BS Public Health), Regional Studies graduate certificate (0 enrolled), School Nurse graduate certificate (0 enrolled), MA International Relations (declining enrollment; new track in MPA being developed). Part of ongoing Ohio SB1 compliance requiring elimination of programs with fewer than 15 graduates over 3 years. WSU previously eliminated 15 programs under SB1 including BA African-American Studies, BA Women and Gender Studies, BA Philosophy, BA Chemistry, and others. 5 new programs approved simultaneously: BS Accelerated Health Sciences, STEM MBA, Classical Cultures minor, Manufacturing and Logistics minor, Operations and Data Analytics minor. Provost James Denniston cited enrollment trends, workforce needs, incoming student interests, HS pathways, and peer institution offerings as decision factors. Spring 2026 commencement: 1,650+ graduates, up YoY in College of Liberal Arts and Lake Campus (+20%).

column2: 19 positions eliminated across IT Services and Luddy School of Informatics
column11: 13 IT Services (UITS) positions eliminated May 1 per VP Kendra Ketchum email — driven by need to align resources with university priorities and ensure long-term financial sustainability. 6 additional Luddy School of Informatics, Computing and Engineering positions eliminated May 29 per Dean Joanna Millunchick email — part of school restructuring to align with evolving university priorities. 19 total confirmed cuts; university declined to confirm broader scope despite social media reports of additional departmental cuts. IU policy requires 30 days written notice; WARN Act 60-day notice applies if total exceeds 50. No WARN filing on Indiana DWD website as of publication. Separate from Indiana HEA 1001 program cuts (April 2026) also in database. Also: IU-licensed public media station WFIU/WTIU cut 4 full-time + 14 part-time positions the same week.

column2: Up to 45 staff layoffs to close $18M FY2027 budget shortfall
column11: President Diacon announced up to 45 layoffs in April 30 "Talk with Todd" campus address; notices going out in coming weeks pending FY2027 budget board approval. VP budgets cut 5-10%. $18M shortfall driven by expected state funding reduction, anticipated enrollment decline, inflation, and significant drop in international students due to federal visa policy changes. 2% raise for all non-union employees also announced. KSU has been reducing budget gradually for 10+ years. Strong enrollment continues in College of Aeronautics and Engineering and fashion design. Total Ohio public university enrollment today roughly same as 2005 but state support (inflation-adjusted) is 27% lower. Diacon cited Penn State (50 major closures), UMD (150 positions), ECU ($25M shortfall), and Clemson as peer institutions facing similar pressures.

column2: 44 academic programs discontinued as part of $25M savings plan
column11: 44 total programs discontinued: 33 voluntarily identified by faculty/administrators + 11 recommended by APRO oversight committee last year. Named programs include: BA Sociology (CIP 45.1101), MAED Middle Grades, MS Software Engineering (CIP 14.0903), MS Sustainable Tourism and Hospitality, PB Sustainable Tourism and Hospitality, Minor Ethnic Studies, Minor Physics (CIP 40.0801), Minor Speech and Hearing, PB Gerontology, BS Family and Consumer Sciences, PB Medical Family Therapy. Currently enrolled students may finish degrees via teach-out. Part of 3-year $25M savings target; first-year goal of $6M+ already exceeded. Additional restructuring: new College of Health and Human Sciences created, library services changed, financial aid and summer school operations updated. Chancellor Philip Rogers cited long-term financial sustainability. Full APRO report at fiscalhealth.ecu.edu.

column2: Radcliffe Institute staff layoffs and role reductions
column11: Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study laid off 4 employees, shifted 3 to part-time, and eliminated 8 vacant positions (15 total roles affected). Institute employs ~100 people. Announced by Dean Tomiko Brown-Nagin via Wednesday email citing "wide range of federal actions targeting Harvard, cost pressures, and market volatility." Harvard central administration directed all units to pursue "structural cuts." Follows prior hiring freeze, salary freeze for non-union employees, and vacant role eliminations. Radcliffe endowment-dependent (86% of revenue). Harvard reported $113M deficit in FY2025 on $6.7B revenue — first deficit since pandemic. New 8% endowment tax (Big Beautiful Bill) projected to cost Harvard $200M+/year. DOJ lawsuit filed alleging Title VI Civil Rights Act violations. FAS departments already asked to plan for up to 20% budget cuts. Brown-Nagin noted uncertainty will last "years, not months."

column2: Susan Polgar Institute for Chess Excellence (SPICE) program eliminated
column11: SPICE (Susan Polgar Institute for Chess Excellence) eliminated after 14 years at Webster (moved from Texas Tech 2012). Program accolades: 2 world championships, 3 Olympiad gold medals, 90+ national titles, 10 Pan-American Intercollegiate championships, 7 Final Four titles; just won 2026 Pan-Am for 13th consecutive President's Cup berth. Head coach GM Liem Le confirmed departure April 30. Program cost $1M+/year from operating budget; university says it raised $0 in outside endowments in 14 years. Reasons cited: unsustainable operating cost during years of losses, enrollment declines (Webster campus enrollment declined by half), and Trump-era visa restrictions (most team members attended on visas; Webster ranks 2nd in Missouri for enrollment decline due to visa restrictions). University posted first net-positive revenue in 10+ years after recent restructuring; chess savings to contribute to fiscal year goals. Program founder Susan Polgar publicly disputed university's account, saying she was never contacted and could have launched fundraising campaign; called closure equivalent to Alabama eliminating football. Program alumni include GMs Wesley So, Ray Robson, and Awonder Liang.

column2: 9 FTE staff positions eliminated to close $2.4M structural deficit
column11: CSU Pueblo eliminated equivalent of ~9 full-time staff positions plus closed 8 vacant positions, reorganized units, and cut athletics budget by $1M to close $2.4M structural deficit. In-state tuition raised 3.5%, out-of-state 5%. Announced by President Rhonda Epper in April 29 budget update. Enrollment fell 3.2% to 6,851 students between 2019-2024. Epper cited "tight competitive market and some negative narratives about the value of higher education" alongside budgetary constraints. Part of broader Colorado higher ed flat-funding crisis driving cuts across the state system.

column2: Men's NCAA Division I tennis program discontinued
column11: Men's tennis discontinued effective end of spring 2026 semester. 8-member roster (2025-26); 5 are seniors with completed eligibility; 3 remaining eligible for transfer portal (opens May 4). Scholarships honored through degree completion. Head coach Maja Kovacek continues coaching women's team (which won MVC championship 2026). Program competed in Summit League for 9 years after MVC dropped men's tennis in 2017; prior 36 years in MVC. Finished 2026 season 9-14, eliminated in Summit League Championship semifinals. Third Division I school to cut tennis in 5 days (after Arkansas April 24 and SLU April 27). Reason: thorough analysis of multiple factors per AD Jeri Beggs; no additional details disclosed. Women's program unaffected.

column2: Men's and women's NCAA Division I tennis programs discontinued
column11: Men's (est. 1975) and women's (est. 1976) NCAA Division I tennis programs discontinued effective immediately following completion of 2025-26 season at Atlantic 10 Conference Championships. 19 total student-athletes (10 men, 9 women); 5 graduating spring 2026; remaining 14 eligible for immediate transfer portal entry under discontinuation-of-sport exception. 2 coaching positions eliminated: head coach James Tobin (full-time, 2nd year) and assistant Emilien Burnel (part-time); staff member Lizzie Barlow also thanked. No on-campus facility; teams played at Dwight Davis Tennis Center and Missouri Athletic Club West. Operating expenses: $173,199 for 2023-24 per Dept. of Education filing. SLU drops to 16 Division I sports (minimum 14 required). First programs cut since men's and women's golf in 2006. Part of national wave: University of Arkansas also dropped tennis same week. Driven by NIL/revenue-sharing era budget pressures.

column2: Up to 150 positions eliminated amid 10% state funding cut and federal research losses
column11: Hiring freeze effective immediately April 27; up to 150 positions eliminated through layoffs, retirements and vacancy eliminations. No new positions created until at least June 30; positions at offer stage may proceed. Travel restricted; contracted services require CFO approval; capital projects limited to essential operations. Driven by 10%+ state funding reduction ($111M cut across University System of Maryland to close $3.3B state deficit) + reduced federal support + rising costs. Total state funding $2.21B for FY2026. UMD among 12 USM schools absorbing cuts alongside UMB (60 positions), UMES, Morgan State, Towson (hiring pause), Bowie State ($18M deficit). Part of systemic Maryland higher ed funding crisis.

Governing board voted to permanently close at end of spring 2026 term. Founded 1946 by Sisters of Saint Anne; Catholic liberal arts institution known for music and art. Enrollment 1,202 as of fall 2024, down 16.6% since 2019. $18.4M long-term debt as of June 2025; endowment assets under $1.4M (all donor-restricted); investments fell ~80% in FY2025. Despite $2M in cost cuts, 7.5% spring enrollment increase, improved fall deposits, and fundraising beating projections, the progress was insufficient. Massachusetts Dept of Higher Education flagged as closure risk in early April 2026 citing inability to verify sufficient resources. Had explored mergers, partnerships, and alternative revenue streams before board vote. Transfer agreements in place with 5 regional colleges. Employees laid off in waves by role. Announcement made on 80th anniversary of founding.

All varsity sports discontinued effective fall 2026 except esports: men's and women's basketball, men's and women's cross country, men's and women's soccer, and women's volleyball eliminated. 13 coaching positions cut this month; no full-time staff affected (coaches with full-time roles retain them). Saves ~$351K annually. 130 total student-athletes; 62 in esports (retained). 68 non-esports athletes affected. Students informed after enrollment deadlines had passed, sparking petition and pushback. College will expand intramural, club sports and wellness programs; women's flag football club retained. Part of broader $5M deficit mitigation for 2026-27; separate actions include 87 staff layoffs, 41 vacant position cuts, 2 faculty retrenchments, and 15 academic program restructurings/eliminations. $128M operating budget adopted April 7. New president Daniel Lufkin begins June 2026.

column2: Four degree programs eliminated amid $4.5M budget cuts
column11: Board of Regents approved elimination of 4 degrees: MS in Education - Higher Education (opposed by Regent Wilmot); BA in Modern Languages - German emphasis (CIP 16.0501); BM in Music Business emphasis; BA in Education - Modern Languages 7-12 German Teaching Endorsement. Chosen for low/declining enrollment and poor long-term viability. ~19 faculty roles cut via voluntary separations, eliminations, and unfilled openings. Additional $2.3M in operational/administrative reductions including graduate assistant reductions and vacating buildings. Part of $40M+ NU system-wide reductions; UNK's share proportional at $4.5M. Enrolled students may finish degrees via teach-out. Third round of UNK program cuts since 2023 (theatre and others eliminated then). UNL separately had 4 departments cut in December 2025.

column2: 7 programs approved for elimination by Iowa Board of Regents
column11: 7 programs approved for elimination by Iowa Board of Regents: BA in African American Studies (CIP 05.0201), BA in Classical Languages, BA in Gender Women's and Sexuality Studies (CIP 05.0207), BA in Italian (CIP 16.0902), BA in Russian (CIP 16.0402), BS in Applied Physics (CIP 40.0801), and MA in African American World Studies (suspended since 2021; no enrolled students for 5 years). Also dissolves two admin units: African American Studies Program and Dept of Gender Women's and Sexuality Studies in College of Liberal Arts and Sciences. Minors in African American and women's studies will continue. French program exempted after faculty grew enrollment above 30. UI found 13 undergrad and 16 grad programs underenrolled but only requested closure of 7. Financial savings described as minimal by regents.

column2: 3 graduate programs approved for closure by Iowa Board of Regents
column11: 3 graduate programs approved for closure by Iowa Board of Regents: MA in Psychology (suspended Fall 2024; no enrolled students), Professional Science Master's in Industrial Mathematics (lost lead faculty 2021; no students since Fall 2019), and a third graduate program (not named in available reporting). Part of board-mandated low-enrollment review (graduate threshold: 10 or fewer students). Financial savings described as minimal. Current enrolled students may finish degrees; no new admissions.

column2: Board voted 4-3 to close two degree programs
column11: Board voted 4-3 to close two degree programs: Criminal Justice (15 students; program supervisor said it generates $100K/year and enrollment was increasing) and Health Information Management (59 students; teach-out arrangement with Klamath Community College). Part of $4.2M budget cuts package for 2026-27 to rebuild ending fund balance to 10% of general fund (currently projected to drop to 3.1% without action). Supervisors of both programs publicly disputed the rationale, calling the process flawed and claiming the programs operate in the black. Student government president criticized lack of student input. College also facing $550K shortfall in current fiscal year. Three-year mitigation plan overall.

Director position (vacant since Pat Tetreault 2024 retirement, budgeted $102K) eliminated. Remaining staff absorbed into Student Culture and Community under Office of Student Life, relocating to Jackie Gaughan Multicultural Center fall 2026. GSC established 2023 via merger of LGBTQA+ Center and Women's Center. Services redistributed: safer sex kits to University Health Center; menstrual products to Husker Pantry; Lavender Closet to Husker Closet; library content to University Library. Monthly STI drop-in testing discontinued entirely. Follows August 2024 elimination of UNL Office of Diversity and Inclusion. Part of broader NU system DEI restructuring.

Cal Athletics laid off ~25 staff in marketing, athletic communications and creative services units, effective early June 2026. Framed as "complete redefinition" of external operations transitioning to new "Strawberry Creek Studios" revenue generation model. Driven by $24.3M projected shortfall for 2024-25 fiscal year and broader college sports landscape changes (conference realignment, transfer portal, NIL). Co-ADs Jenny Simon-O'Neill and Jay Larson announced cuts April 11. Athletics department action; no academic programs affected. New football coach Tosh Lupoi hired December 2025.

Additionally cutting 41 already-vacant positions. Driven by flat state appropriations (3 consecutive years), 1.8% projected enrollment decline, and 11% rising healthcare costs. York campus buildings being sold. Budget deficit projected near $10M without intervention.

column2: Main campus in Fort Pierce, FL closed
column11: Main campus in Fort Pierce, FL closed April 15, 2026 with 40-50 layoffs (instructors, administrators, facilities staff). Students notified April 9 — just 6 days before closure. ~260 students enrolled fall 2024. Programs offered: 1-year commercial pilot ($68K+) and 2-year aviation associate degree ($115K+). Parent company attributed closure to lawsuit by former student's family, failed sale, and possible bankruptcy. Accrediting Commission of Career Schools and Colleges (ACCSC) had voted to withdraw accreditation fall 2025 following two fatal flight crashes (2023, 2024) and anonymous complaints of widespread violations including safety, faculty qualifications, enrollment agreements, and student services. As of Jan 2025, 91% of students were 100+ days behind on required flight time. College was appealing accreditation withdrawal. Kissimmee branch campus (aviation maintenance program) remains open; its accreditation withdrawal also under appeal. College said refunds to be provided and working with other schools for student transfer options.
column13: Aviator College of Aeronautical Science and Technology

column2: 10 degree programs eliminated and 13 consolidated under Iowa Board of Regents mandate
column11: Provost Jason Keith announced April 2 elimination of 10 degree programs and consolidation of 13 others following Iowa Board of Regents Workforce Alignment Review. Programs closed include undergrad: BS Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (CIP 26.1103), BS Environmental Studies (CIP 03.0103), BS Interdisciplinary Design, BS Religious Studies (CIP 38.0201), BS Women's and Gender Studies (CIP 05.0207); grad: MS/PhD Accounting Analytics, PhD Biophysics, PhD Energy Systems Engineering, PhD Interdisciplinary Graduate Studies, PhD Toxicology. Programs consolidated/merged: 4 physics PhDs (applied, condensed matter, high energy, nuclear) → 1 degree; Sociology + Rural Sociology → 1 graduate program; Earth Science + Geology → 1 program at each level; Rhetoric Composition and Professional Communication merged into larger program; graduate Gerontology merged into College of Health and Human Sciences program; Experiential Graphic Design consolidated into multi-credential pathway. 7 programs exempted despite low enrollment (nursing, veterinary science, math/science education). 15 programs given 2-year extension. Board of Regents approval June 15 meeting. Courses in many closed subjects continue via minors/certificates. Part of same Iowa Board of Regents review that cut programs at University of Iowa (7 programs) and University of Northern Iowa (3 programs) — both already in database.

column2: 11 programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
column11: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1 to act on 11 Indiana State programs. Named cuts include: Master of Music, MA Geography, MS Genetic Counseling, MA Industrial Technology. Part of statewide HEA 1001 compliance cutting 584 programs across 7 Indiana public universities. Students enrolled in suspended/eliminated programs may finish degrees; new admissions cease fall 2026; full elimination by fall 2027.

column2: 10 programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
column11: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1 to act on 10 Ivy Tech programs. Named cuts include: associate degrees in public safety, nanotechnology, and machine repair. Ivy Tech had fewest programs flagged statewide (47 reviewed; only 10 acted upon). Part of statewide HEA 1001 compliance cutting 584 programs across 7 Indiana public universities. New Indiana law also updates Ivy Tech governance and doubles down on workforce mission.

93 programs sunsetted (closed or paused) out of ~460 total following 7-month academic portfolio review begun August 2025. Breakdown: 41 bachelor's degrees, 19 graduate degrees, 33 certificates (28 advanced). 55 of the 93 had zero enrolled students. 258 students affected (1.2% of 22K+ enrollment); all may complete degrees via teach-out. No positions eliminated. Affected programs include classics, ceramics, sculpture, painting, German, Italian, French, Russian, Middle Eastern studies, African American studies, digital humanities, Modern Jewish studies, and others. Driven by enrollment concentration: 34% of programs serve 80% of students. Explicitly not a cost-cutting exercise per provost. Chancellor Kent Syverud departing May 10 for University of Michigan.

MADE (Minorities Achieving Dreams of Excellence) student support program closing end of spring 2026 semester after 7 years. Founded 2019 as a president's office initiative to support underserved first-year students. Program coordinator Jason Perry also departing after graduation. Program offered early orientation, scholarships, monthly meetings, coaching, mentoring, study space, ambassadorships, and internships. Had 200+ students with 90%+ retention rate as of 2023. Cited reasons: UM financial crisis and broader national trend of state bills targeting DEI/equity programs. Separate from February 2026 board vote eliminating 16 minors and concentrations.

Multiple program discontinuations and restructurings as UNO transitions to LSU New Orleans in 2026. Discontinued: BA International Studies (→ minor), BS Elementary Ed & Special Ed (Grades 1-5), MAT Elementary Ed & Special Ed (Grades 1-5), MAT Secondary Ed & Special Ed (Grades 6-12), MFA theatre-related tracks/concentrations. Restructured: BA Art History → BA Studio Art (Art History as minor); BA Film and Theatre → BA Film Arts (Theatre Arts as minor); MFA renamed. Taught out: BS Mathematics (while new BS Data Science is developed); MS Tax Accounting (existing teach-out continues). MA Arts Administration merged into MPA. Less than 2% of students affected. All faculty retained during transition. New programs under development: engineering management, hospitality and tourism, data science, healthcare management.

column2: 4 programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
column11: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1 to act on 4 USI programs — fewest of any Indiana institution. Named cuts include: AS Early Childhood Education, MA Liberal Studies, undergraduate Electronic Business degree, Master in Social Health Services and Allied Professions. Part of statewide HEA 1001 compliance cutting 584 programs across 7 Indiana public universities.

column2: Programs suspended or eliminated under Indiana HEA 1001 mandate
column11: Indiana Commission for Higher Education voted April 1; Vincennes University participated in statewide HEA 1001 compliance review. Specific program names not detailed in available reporting. Part of statewide action cutting 584 programs across all 7 Indiana public universities. Vincennes reported costs by cost center rather than individual program level per CHE reporting options.

column2: Senior leadership layoffs and executive restructuring to close $40M deficit
column11: Three senior administrators laid off March 31: Jerry Tarrer (former interim president/CEO, at college since 2017), Laurent Pernot (VP of strategic partnerships, previously chief of staff for 8 years), Jeffrey Reuter (associate VP of budget, planning and analysis since 2019). CIO Kathie Koch also departed same month. Part of broader restructuring announced by President Shantay Bolton including hiring freeze for nonessential admin positions and further spending cuts. Since January 2025: 48 full-time faculty laid off (32 tenured); year prior: 70 staff cut. Total deficit: $40M. Bolton also simultaneously added new administrators: Emmanuel Lalande (SVP enrollment strategy), Adriel Hilton (chief of staff), Maryann Schaefer (AVP admissions), Aubrie Willaert (VP development), Jeffrey Bethke (interim CFO), Adam Weiss (VP legal affairs). Restructuring shifting oversight to five deans per May 2, 2026 follow-up article. Implementation continues through fiscal year ending August 31, 2026. No further faculty layoffs currently planned per Provost McBride, though not ruled out if enrollment declines.

Non-renewal letters sent by Provost Dr. Ryan Sandefer citing "current financial constraints" and institutional restructuring. Sources indicate more than a dozen faculty affected; college declined to confirm any personnel figures. College described cuts as "necessary budget adjustments." Letters stated non-renewals do not reflect negatively on performance. Catholic Benedictine private institution in Duluth, MN. Student sit-in protest reported following cuts including a popular philosophy professor.

Board unanimously voted to eliminate 10 career and technical education (CTE) programs, including all architecture programs and one certificate each from several other academic areas. Reasons cited: low enrollment, non-transferable credits, low completion rates, and lack of industry demand. No full-time faculty negatively impacted; no adjuncts losing jobs as they typically teach across multiple programs. Budget pressures driven by statewide tuition freeze and declining property tax revenue from appraisal freeze. Chancellor LeBlanc described cuts as addressing "obsolete" programs amid a "new reality" for the college budget.

All 9 staff at Keller Center for Innovation in Engineering Education laid off. Tenured faculty salaries frozen; all other staff raises capped at 1%. All departments cut 5-10% of budgets. Most staff hiring frozen. Driven by revised endowment return projection (8% vs historical 10.2-12%), translating to ~$11.3B less in endowment value over 10 years and ~$500M less in annual payouts. Additional pressures: rising healthcare costs, federal research grant suspensions, new 8% endowment tax. Endowment funds 65% of operating budget ($36.4B total). President Eisgruber warned more cuts are coming. Graduate stipends and undergraduate financial aid commitments preserved.

Library Director Dan McClure (9-year tenure) laid off effective March 19 with no reason given — college's only credentialed librarian (MLS degree). College plans to hire a part-time replacement; no timeline given. Around the same time, Automotive Repair and Historic Preservation & Restoration programs also eliminated. ~800 students enrolled. Driven by budget shortfall as costs rise faster than incoming funds. McClure taught Library Research Skills (1-credit information literacy course each quarter) and managed interlibrary loans, Open Educational Resources compliance (Oregon law), vendor contracts, and consortium memberships (Oregon Community College Library Association, Chinook Library Network).

70+ programs, minors and certificates cut or consolidated to address $45M deficit. Major cuts: all linguistics degrees phased out (dept merged with World Languages, Literatures and Cultures effective Sept. 1); BA in Latino and Latin American Studies eliminated; MA in Women's and Gender Studies cut. 25 undergraduate minors eliminated including women's and gender studies, LGBTQ studies, Mexican American studies, Africana studies, Asian studies, dance, geology, and special education. 40+ certificate programs cut (avg. fewer than 2 students/year). Driven by sharp decline in international enrollment and reduced state funding. Faculty buyouts offered to those with 15+ years service (deadline April 10). Linguistics dept chair said faculty were not consulted. Faculty and staff impact TBD. Enrolled students may complete degrees; no new admissions to affected programs. ~47,000 total enrollment.

17 programs sunset per Ohio Advance Higher Education Act (SB1) mandate requiring 5+ annual degree conferrals averaged over 3 years. Originally 36 programs fell below threshold; 16 approved to merge with similar programs, 3 received ODHE waivers, 17 sunset. Programs closed include BA in African American Studies, BA in French, BA in Chemistry, BA in Dance, BFA in Interdisciplinary Arts, BM in Music Therapy, BA in Mathematics, BA in Physics, BA in Geological Sciences, and several associate degrees. Most disciplines continue via minors, BS alternatives or related programs. 16 additional programs being merged/combined. Currently enrolled students may complete degrees as outlined. Incoming applicants to be notified of alternatives.

column2: 14 classified positions eliminated across 3 campuses amid $1.8M structural deficit
column11: Board approved 9 classified positions eliminated at Contra Costa College (CCC): academic scheduling specialist, instructional assistant counseling/matriculation, office assistant II fine/media arts, program assistant welcome center/outreach, program coordinator dramatic arts, dean of enrollment services (cut next year), learning disabilities specialist DSPS, wellness coordinator, plus additional vacant positions. 6 positions cut at Diablo Valley (2 grant-funded), 1 at Los Medanos (14 total across district). Undocumented students program coordinator position initially included then reversed after student/community pressure. 120 layoff notices issued via bumping process; 69 subsequently rescinded as of April 30. Structural deficit $1.8M current year, worsening in future years. District gave 8% merit raises to top administrators in 2025 — criticized by union. Contra Costa College serves more vulnerable population (San Pablo area) but received disproportionate cuts. Wellness coordinator loss also eliminates 3 student worker positions. Local 1 SEIU represents classified staff. Board failed first vote March 13, called emergency meeting March 15 to approve under deadline.

Board of Trustees voted to permanently close the college at the end of Fall 2026. Announced by President Jennifer Chrisler on March 14, 2026. Driven by $20M+ in debt, $3.7M operating deficit (2025), chronic enrollment decline since 2019 (when college did not admit an incoming class), and NECHE accreditor sustainability requirement. Five-year sustainability plan (2019-2024) fell short: raised $55M of $60M goal but could not grow enrollment sufficiently. Two student pathways offered: Completion (Division III students finish at Hampshire through Dec 2026) and Transfer (to Five College Consortium partners and others). Founded 1965; known for independent liberal arts model. Board stated closure decision came only after exhausting all alternatives; nearly all trustees are alumni.

column2: School of Public Health staff and lecturer layoffs amid FY2027 budget shortfall
column11: School of Public Health conducting Reduction in Force (RIF) including mid-contract lecturer layoffs and staff cuts. Lecturer Lex Eisenberg received layoff notice March 13 mid-contract. ~50 students, faculty and staff demonstrated April 22 outside annual awards ceremony demanding halt to cuts and financial transparency. Compensation allocation cut from $39.3M (FY2025) to $37M (FY2026); FY2027 shortfall projected. Root causes: 65-student drop in international enrollment 2024-25 (accelerating due to Trump travel ban affecting 19 countries and visa scrutiny); declining indirect cost recovery from federal research disruptions; 2023 one-time $2M investment in faculty/staff pay (including 19 new tenure-track faculty) created unsustainable compensation baseline. School relies ~80% on tuition and indirect cost recovery. Dean Corliss stated school remains committed to "world-class education and research." Interim Associate Dean Kidwell confirmed compensation increases and layoffs are structurally separate decisions. Epidemiology PhD admissions also paused for 2025-26 cycle due to NIH grant terminations (separate prior action).

column2: Spanish degree (eliminated) and Medical Laboratory Science degree (suspended)
column11: UMaine announced it will end its Spanish degree program and suspend new admissions to the Medical Laboratory Science degree, citing an $18M structural deficit. The university is also cutting $5.6M in costs and laying off staff. A Budget Town Hall was held March 23, 2026.

column2: 7 classified positions eliminated gutting College to Career and Student Success programs
column11: Board voted March 10 to eliminate 7 classified positions: 2 from College to Career (C2C) program (Mary Schexnaydre, student success coach 15 years; Noah Morris, employment services advisor 13 years) and 5 from Student Success program. C2C program goes from coordinator + 2 specialists to coordinator only. 23 new students joining C2C fall 2026 who were promised services that no longer exist. Program was named most successful in California in 2018, placing students into 400+ jobs. Budget driven: combined Morris/Schexnaydre salaries ($124,139) replaced by upgraded coordinator role costing $205,429 — net loss of 2 specialists with no budget savings. Part of $10M deficit multi-year strategy including executive pay cuts, hiring freeze, furloughs. Driven by declining enrollment and state funding. SEIU Local 1021 involved. Staff said DOR contract compliance at risk without specialized disability expertise.

column2: Dance program eliminated; two legacy programs cut; 52 staff laid off
column11: Portland State declared a financial crisis amid a $35M deficit and declining enrollment (down ~25% since 2010). PSU eliminated dance programming (April 2026), cut two additional legacy programs, and laid off 52 faculty and staff (confirmed May 14, 2026 by OPB). The university is also evaluating cuts or consolidations across 19 academic departments.

column2: Downtown Center campus closed after 47 years
column11: Downtown Center at 88 Fourth St (Fourth and Mission) closing after spring 2026; no classes scheduled for fall 2026. Campus opened 1979; 47 years old. Enrollment of 152 full-time equivalent students — far below California state minimum of 1,000 required to receive $2.2M annual state funding. 900 part-time students also affected. Culinary, fashion, and language classes relocated to under-enrolled campuses including Chinatown/North Beach Center. No employee job losses. College owns 84,000 sq ft building; exploring partnerships with educational institutions, community orgs, and the city. Downtown location increasingly isolated near shuttered SF Centre mall; English learners also scattered by ICE enforcement fears. CCSF enrollment has fallen from ~22,000 full-time equivalent students a decade ago to ~9,000 currently.

NJCU announced the reduction of its academic portfolio by 37 percent, which involved sunsetting 48 undergraduate programs, 24 minors, 28 graduate programs, 10 certificate programs, and one doctoral program.

At least 16 faculty laid off, mostly in humanities, effective end of academic year (pay and benefits through August). Board of trustees approved cuts in early February 2026. Driven by Ohio Advance Higher Education Act (SB1) compliance — requires eliminating programs with fewer than 5 graduates/year over 3 years — and ongoing fiscal distress including a $26M student tuition/fee backlog. Ohio Dept. of Higher Education placed CSU on fiscal watch in 2024. Prior year cuts included 33 staff and 7 faculty. HBCU; secured $400K+ in emergency student aid via UNCF partnership in January 2026.

Labouré College of Healthcare (founded 1892, 134 years) will cease all academic operations August 31, 2026. Board of Directors unanimously approved merger/acquisition agreement with Curry College (~4 miles away in Milton, MA). Nursing programs will transfer to Curry's School of Nursing and Health Sciences under a new unit called the Labouré Center for Advancing Healthcare Opportunity. Reasons cited: persistent financial and enrollment challenges, and regulatory hurdles (state regulators voted to shut down nursing program in 2023 after students failed 80% first-time NCLEX pass rate threshold; decision overturned on appeal; scores restored to full approval by May 2024). Enrollment declined from peak of 1,188 (fall 2020) to 530 (fall 2024), roughly a 55% drop. Only 168 new students enrolled in 2025 vs. goal of 300. ASN nursing students (majority of enrollment) will transfer to Curry's Milton campus in fall 2026; tuition and fees held at 2026-2027 Labouré rates; credits transfer seamlessly. Students in other programs (e.g. respiratory care) being directed to articulation agreements at other institutions if unable to complete by Aug. 31. Curry plans to hire ~15 Labouré nursing faculty and ~20 staff (35-40 total of ~100 total Labouré employees). As of Nov. 1, 2024: 23 FT instructional employees, 49 noninstructional staff at Labouré. Labouré endowment pledged to support the new Center. Labouré plans to sell its physical property (303 Adams St, Milton — former Aquinas College campus) and use proceeds to fund the Center. Curry enrolled ~2,000 students in fall 2024 and also faced enrollment declines; acquisition expected to potentially double Curry nursing enrollment. Deal subject to regulatory approval at time of announcement.
