column11: Board unanimously voted to eliminate 9 minors and 7 concentrations (16 total), saving ~$400K. Minors cut include African American Studies, Cybersecurity, Economics, Latin American Studies, Management Information Systems, Non-profit Studies, Peace and Justice Studies, Philosophy and Religion, and Professional Writing. Current students with declared minors/concentrations may finish via teach-out. Second round of cuts after 6 programs were eliminated in May 2025. Part of effort to close ~$8M shortfall. Combined with fee increases, generates ~$800K. 4 athletic teams (men's/women's swimming and tennis) also recommended for elimination but decision deferred to May 2026 board meeting. Tuition increase not pursued for 2026-27.

Board voted 4-2 to lay off 16 non-faculty workers and eliminate 17 vacant positions (33 total). Adaptive Physical Education (APE) program discontinued beginning 2026-27; offered for 40+ years serving ~200 disabled students. Cuts also include 3 Disability Support Programs roles. Driven by loss of HSI federal grants, stagnating state funding, and local property tax underperformance. Projected deficit of $3.75M in 2027 and $4.4M in 2028 without action. Board declared financial hardship via resolution.

387 total employees losing jobs via WARN filing: 26 assistant professors, 106 adjuncts, 14 head coaches, ~31 federal work-study students, ~49 student employees, and remaining admin/staff. Terminations begin May 15 through Sept. 30, 2026. Founded 1958 by Sisters of St. Francis of Sylvania; owned and subsidized by Sisters for nearly 25 years. Closure driven by declining enrollment, rising costs, and unsustainable funding model. President William Bisset stepped down; Sister Nancy Linenkugel named 13th and final president. Teach-out agreements with University of Toledo (dedicated transfer process), Walsh University, Trine University, and Marietta College. ~1,200 students affected. No bumping rights or union representation for laid-off staff.

column2: 60 staff layoffs and 10 vacant positions eliminated to address $17.5M structural deficit
column11: Board voted February 9 to lay off ~60 classified staff and eliminate equivalent of ~10 vacant positions. All 49 classified management and 46 academic administrator positions also opened to potential elimination in coming weeks restructuring. Structural deficit projected to reach $17.5M in FY2027 nearly wiping out reserves. College scraped together $6.3M in one-off funds reducing current deficit to $5.8M. Trustee blowback during Feb 9 meeting. Part of broader California community college funding crisis.

Deactivating 1 undergraduate program (Environmental Geography, B.S.), 2 graduate programs (Conflict Analysis and Resolution, M.S.; Higher Education and Student Affairs Administration, M.S.), 2 minors, and 3 certificates. 19 students in impacted bachelor's programs, 29 in master's programs (48 total; 0.8% of enrollment). Enrolled students may complete degrees via teach-out. Part of SUNY-mandated Framework for Fiscal Stability Plan targeting elimination of $16-17M structural deficit by 2027-28. Deficit attributed to Great Recession-era state cuts and COVID-19 financial losses. Prior year cuts included sociology. Faculty union UUP held campus rally March 10 demanding state funding.

column2: Permanent institution closure after 20 years of operation
column11: Board of Trustees voted February 7, 2026 to cease academic operations at end of 2025-2026 academic year. Founded 2002, incorporated in CA; first class admitted 2005; Reformed Christian liberal arts institution in Old Town Pasadena. Closure driven by declining enrollment, rising operational costs (Southern California), heightened accreditation expectations, and loss of federal funds. Accreditation held by WASC Senior (on probation at time of closure). Over half of full-time students scheduled to graduate May 2026; teach-out agreements established with local Christian colleges and sister institutions for underclassmen. Staff and faculty given advance notice to find next positions. Board explored decreased operational expenses, additional student recruitment, and campus relocation before concluding closure was only remaining option. Source is the official college closure announcement page.

22 staff laid off (18 full-time, 4 part-time) via reorganizations, staffing consolidations and reductions across administrative offices. Majority are non-student-facing roles. No faculty affected. Enrollment has dropped from 2,033 in 2011-12 to 1,600+ currently. Driven by declining birth rates, fewer students choosing college, and reduced international enrollment. Endowment remains strong at ~$370M. Board of Trustees approved to return college to balanced budget.

45 total positions eliminated (12 faculty, 21 staff, 11 administrators; ~40% currently vacant). College of Education (est. 1958) dissolved and absorbed into new College of Humanities, Education and Social Science (CHESS), saving ~$1.8M. Biology dept split: biochemistry, microbiology, and anatomy & physiology merged with pharmacy's pharmaceutical sciences into new Dept of Biomedical Sciences under Kasiska Division of Health Sciences. Driven by $8M deficit from 3% state-mandated budget cut plus $3M health insurance increases and $2.2M in unfunded cost adjustments. Accreditation concerns raised by former College of Education dean.

All ~40 college-employed dining staff positions eliminated after spring 2026 semester; staff may apply to continue with dining contractor Bon Appétit. Early retirement incentive offered to all employees 60+ with 10+ years of service (2 weeks pay per year worked, up to 18 months). Driven by missed enrollment goals for 2 consecutive years. No faculty positions affected. Tuition benefit preserved for early retirees with currently enrolled dependents.

SMC eliminating ~70 classified and management positions in response to $16.7M projected deficit that could deplete financial reserves by 2026-27, after already implementing $8.6M in prior budget reductions. Declining enrollment drives the shortfall. Cuts target classified staff and management; no faculty layoffs announced at this stage.

Women's and Gender Studies (WGST) program closed effective immediately per Interim President Tommy Williams. Impacts BA/BS degrees, undergraduate minor, and graduate certificate. 25 enrolled majors and 31 enrolled minors (56 total) will be taught out over up to 6 semesters. 50+ affiliated faculty employment status unaffected. Cited Texas A&M System policy compliance and limited enrollment. Part of broader spring 2026 course review covering ~5,400 syllabi; 6 courses also canceled for non-compliance.

WSU Athletics eliminated five staff positions in late January 2026 to "structure and right-size" its operations. Cuts driven by financial pressures from the House vs. NCAA settlement, which requires universities to directly compensate student-athletes. AD Kevin Saal had requested $1M in NIL donations in April 2025 to support men's basketball. Cuts coincided with KU and K-State also seeking government assistance for athletic funding. Broader context: WSU also announced a 7% general use budget cut ($7.9M reduction for next fiscal year), and the College of Engineering had eliminated at least seven employees in December 2025. WSU had record enrollment but noted headcount alone does not translate to revenue growth.

column2: Admissions paused for 5 Ph.D. programs for fall 2026
column11: Admissions paused for fall 2026 in 5 Ph.D. programs: Clinical Psychology, Anthropology, Human Paleobiology, Political Science, and Mathematics. Applicants notified week of Jan 19; application fees refunded; offered consideration for master's programs instead. University cited need to limit new funding commitments to protect existing Ph.D. student packages. Not described as permanent closure. Separately, total Ph.D. packages across all Columbian College of Arts & Sciences departments also slashed (GWU declined to confirm details). Clinical Psych admitted record-low 3 students fall 2025 (typical: 8-9); APA cohort size requirements led to zero admits rather than partial cohort. Math had zero remaining funding after covering continuing students. Human Paleobiology admits ~3/year; timing tied to current student graduation. International enrollment down ~13% of total fall 2025; Trump-era visa/travel changes cited. President Granberg ordered all schools to prepare FY2027 budget contingency plans.

Eastern Washington University announced the discontinuation of its Division I adaptive athletics program (wheelchair basketball) at the end of the 2025-26 academic season due to sustainability and financial challenges. The program was the first of its kind in the Pacific Northwest.

California College of the Arts closing permanently end of 2026-27 academic year after 119 years. Founded 1907 in East Bay; moved to SF Design District campus ($123M building opened 2025). Vanderbilt University acquiring SF campus and original Oakland property; will establish own undergraduate and graduate programming. CCA Institute and Wattis Institute of Contemporary Arts museum preserved at campus. No current CCA faculty guaranteed jobs under Vanderbilt. 28 non-faculty staff positions eliminated end of spring 2026 semester (mostly union workers). Driven by $20M structural deficit, years of enrollment decline, and tuition-dependent model unsustainable at ~$100M operating budget. Despite $22.5M in private donations in 2025 (matched by Nvidia CEO Jen-Hsun Huang Foundation) and $20M gift — all stop-gap measures. Students graduating by end of 2026-27 receive CCA degrees; others must transfer. No new students admitted fall 2027. Closes same year as prior Bay Area art school wave: SFAI (2022), Mills College merger with Northeastern (2022). Mayor Daniel Lurie attended press conference alongside Vanderbilt Chancellor Diermeier. Last standalone art and design college in San Francisco.

column2: NCAA Division I women's equestrian program eliminated — replaced by STUNT varsity program
column11: Athletic Director Rocko DeLuca announced January 9 elimination of NCAA Division I women's equestrian team effective end of 2025-26 season — team had just won its third conference championship (undefeated season). 33 student-athletes affected. Program transitioned to club sport; STUNT simultaneously elevated from club to NCAA varsity status. Decision made primarily on budget grounds citing $1M+ annual savings. Three active lawsuits alleging fraud and misrepresentation: parents' suit (filed Feb 9), wire fraud investigation by UC Davis police department (AD DeLuca continued soliciting donations after decision was made internally), Title IX concerns (program elevated to D1 as part of Title IX settlement, then eliminated despite championship success while men's programs retained). Independent audit commissioned by parents found original cost report over-estimated expenses by 120%+ ($850K+) — alleged budget inflation through misrepresenting operating expenses, removing legitimate revenue, counting fictional offset as real expense. Metadata on consultant report shows it was completed after the decision was made — used to justify not inform. UC Davis chancellor ordered 10% budget cuts February 2025; equestrian placed on chopping block March 2025 internally; public announcement January 2026 after months of continued recruiting and donation solicitation. UC Davis reviewing its own financial records; findings due June 30 (team's final day). 30 horses donated to program by community members face uncertain future. Parents offered privately funded endowment to sustain program — university rejected offer.
Program suspended after multiple seasons of losses, financial unsustainability, and media investigations. Head coach Desmond Gumbs stepped down; intent to return in Division II.
Restructuring to address structural budget imbalances, cutting 33 positions and redesigning 30 others as part of $4 million realignment.

column2: 109 positions eliminated including 45 teaching faculty amid $18M budget cuts
column11: 109 total positions reduced: 47 eliminated/non-renewed Dec 18 (25 teaching faculty incl. 5 tenured, 22 admin faculty), plus 31 from hiring freeze since May 2025, 22 voluntary separations/incentivized retirements, 9 recent retirements. 45 teaching faculty + 64 admin faculty/staff total. Non-tenured staff/admin conclude June 30, 2026; tenured faculty conclude June 30, 2027 (or early retirement option). Earlham was Wayne County's 7th-largest employer (388 total employees pre-cuts). Structural cash-flow deficit of ~$15M/year for nearly a decade; board mandated balanced budget by 2030 requiring $18M in recurring expense cuts. Follow-up April 2026: some majors confirmed ended per March 30 president email.

Layoffs follow the lifting of financial probation by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools (SACSCOC). Affected faculty represent multiple academic departments at the Memphis institution.

Manuel, Provost Salma Ghanem, and CFO. DePaul has faced declining enrollment and rising costs for several years; layoffs framed as necessary for structural financial sustainability.

column2: MBA program and institution permanently closing after 80 years

Eligible students may apply for Closed School Loan Discharge. Institution continues non-academic operations via Lake Forest Center for Leadership (leadership development consulting). Announced via LinkedIn post and letter to students and faculty December 13-14, 2025. University announced 50 staff layoffs and elimination of 30 to 50 vacant positions due to $7 million projected shortfall driven by enrollment decline and state funding cuts.

column2: Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey campus and programs wound down
